I have a confession to make - INCEPTION is one of my favorite Christopher Nolan films - and, perhaps, it is in my list of TOP 10 ALL TIME FAVORITE films, so this might not be a fair and impartial review of the film. To be fair to me, I did make a conscience effort whilst watching this movie to scrape away my previous preconceptions and opinions of this film and just let it wash over me in this "new light" of my blog to see what my reaction is.My reaction: I LOVE THIS FILM!!!I was asked how far back do you have to go before you can consider a film a "classic" and, I guess, I'd have to say 2010, for this film - to me - is a classic.In INCEPTION, Nolan, and his co-writer brother Jonathan Nolan, go into the dreamworld with the premise that we can join in "shared dreams" to extract information from people that are locked away deep in their conscious (or in some cases unconscious) minds. This film deals with the idea of "Inception", planting an idea into someone's mind. This is, in essence, a "heist" film where our team of heroes is constantly at war with the minds they are inhabiting (since they are seen as parasites). The clock is ticking and they must get in and get out before they get lost.Speaking of time, Nolan - once again - plays with the idea of time in this film. Once you go into a dream, 1 minute is like 1 hour and when you go into a dream of a dream, then 1 minute is like 60 hours and when you go into a dream within a dream within a dream, then...well...you get the idea.If someone loses their way in this film, it's because they are trying to make logical sense of a dream world that defies physics - and time. My suggestion to you is to let go and let the movie take you to some fantastical places - with some fantastical imagery and plot machinations - that I enjoyed the heck out of.Helping out this film is that it is impeccably cast. Leonardo DiCaprio is Cobb the head of this group that enters the dream realm. He is perfectly cast and Nolan, and this film, relies on his likeableness, his charm and the feeling that something just isn't quite right with him. All to very good effect. Ellen Page is strong as Ariadne, the rookie of the team that is our eyes and ears into this world. Ken Watanabe brings his typically strong game to the role of Saito - the man that gives the team the job and goes along for the ride. Nolan regular Cillian Murphy is a welcome addition as the person who they are trying to "Incept" and even small parts are filled with wonderful character actors like the late great, Pete Postlethwaite, Tom Berenger and good ol' Michael Caine.But it is the emergence of two of the co-stars that, up until this film I thought were "fair actors but not great" that really elevates this film for me. Joseph Gordon-Levitt was always the "long haired kid from 3RD ROCK FROM THE SUN", but in this - as Cobb's right-hand man Arthur - he excels and really jumps out of the film as a screen presence. Of course, it really helps him that he has one of the best action sequences - for the most part practically shot - that I have ever scene. And, of course, there's TOM HARDY. He is a movie star and really shows it in the supporting role of Eames. This guy will win an Oscar one day, probably for a film that Nolan Directs him in.My only quibble - and it is a QUIBBLE - is that I didn't really feel any strong chemistry between Marion Cotillard's Mal and DiCaprio's Cobb. She was supposed to be the big "love of his life" and I just didn't sense that. She was very good - and imposing - as she infiltrated Cobb's mind (which is, I think, the purpose of her character), but I could have used a little more between her and DiCaprio. But...as I say...a quibble.All in all, a terrific - different - film. One that I am calling a "classic".Letter Grade: A+10 stars (out of 10) and you can take that to the Bank(ofMarquis)

Reviews: Makes The Matrix look like a playground!
main_review:
Inception is one of these rare experiences I just miss in most movies of today.
It deals with something that everybody does and everybody can not turn off: Dreaming.
It offers so many groundbreaking ideas and fills the movie with memorable and great characters. I am not that big of a Leonardo di Caprio Fan, but this time his acting was completely superb. Tom Hardy & Ellen Page as supporting actors fits perfectly in to the cast.
The movie pacing is awesome, the story is gripping, compelling and very exciting up to the point that you have literally no guarantee or confidence what happens, how or why. Furthermore the visuals (and even action scenes) are straight up stunning. 
Christopher Nolan has again created another ingenious chess game with so much room for speculation or interpretation.
In the end, the question has nothing to do with the "real" or "fake" dream world. It is just how far would you go to finally get what you want and how deep can a catastrophe of the past hunt you down and destroy you.
Is it sometimes a little bit confusing? Yes. Does it sometimes have too much ideas, but only follows them ineffectual? Yes. And that is the only problem Inception has. Because of the (in the end 5) dream worlds, we forget what happens in "reality" and that makes the ending and climax scene look a little bit out of place. All in all, Inception is a brilliant movie, that technically is not quite a perfect 10/10, but also better than an excellent 9/10. The perfect score for it would be a 9.5/10 but since that is impossible, I'm downgrading it: 9/0

Reviews: My favorite Nolan film to date...
main_review: Plot Inception is a heist film that features Leonardo DiCaprio as a Dominic "Dom" Cobb who has been forced to leave the States due to a murder conviction. This event leaves him desperately trying to find his way back to his kids, while pulling one extraction job after another just to make ends meet. These are no ordinary extraction jobs, however, since Cobb is using a highly experimental military technology that allows him to infiltrate the mind of his target and ultimately manipulate that person into giving him the information that he needs to successfully complete the mission. When Cobb's first job in the film goes wrong and he fails in his assignment, he is ultimately forced to work with a Japanese billionaire businessman, played by Ken Watanabe, who promises Cobb a chance to finally return to America and be with his children. The biggest catch of the deal is that Cobb must pull off a job that is otherwise considered impossible to do. He must plant an idea into the mind of his target, played by Cillian Murphy, that will compel the latter to make a major business decision that would disband his father's energy company, a method known as Inception. The CastingThe casting for this film is spot on. Leonardo DiCaprio is unforgettable as a broken, yet highly clever and experienced extractor of information who just wants to go home and be reunited with his family.Cobb's right-hand man, Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is very suave and competent in his field as he as constantly attempts to appeal to Cobb's more logical reasoning by offering up a more realistic viewpoint of the latter's situation. Arthur is particularly skeptical of not only Saito's intentions but also of whether Inception is even a possibility. Believing the mission to be a massive failure from the start, Arthur tries to convince Cobb to simply walk away from the job, despite Saito's irresistibly tempting offer.The rest of the casting in Inception is perfect. Christopher Nolan couldn't have done a better a job of assigning these roles if he'd tried. PacingThe movie includes an excellent combination of fast-paced action scenes and a more deeply written story that focuses on the individual development, agendas, and flaws of some of the characters. Nolan's approach to exploring the sub- consciousness of one's mind and how it can be manipulated by an outside force is enough to make me appreciate the unexpected twists and turns in the plot itself as my mind races and my heart continues to pump nonstop throughout the course of the film all the way to the end.The StoryIt's so easy to make an action film all about the action or to make a deep, emotional film all about the story and maybe not include enough action, but that isn't a problem for Inception. Nolan gives us a compelling story that focuses on the visceral depth of the characters and the challenges that they face throughout the course of the film, while simultaneously using the action only to support the continuous flow of the story, instead of overshadowing it with too many pointless explosions, fight, and/or car chase scenes. Yes, the film does include all of this, but it is never overwhelming or entirely pointless. The Story With Inception, we get a fresh, complete original and engaging story that never fails to impress. Personally, I feel that it leaves me with an ending the makes me think about the limitations of my imagination and where I can go with that imagination if I just knock down the barriers that would otherwise keep me from going to distance and beyond with my own vision. From beginning to end, the story keeps the viewers guessing. It keeps them wondering and, therefore, constantly trying to figure out what is real and what is just another part of the dream. It will force you to ask questions, intelligent questions that could alone prove to be a roller-coaster ride of a trip for the mind itself. What is real? What isn't real? Is any of it real, or are all the characters in this film leaving in one big dream world? These are the questions that I find myself asking during and after watching this masterpiece of a film. Visual AppealVisually, the greatest highlights of the film were of course the city scene, which showed us a dreamed-up Paris bending into itself, and the hotel scene, which showed us constantly rotating and shifting environment that basically said, "Reality, what's that?" Watching a film like Inception, I can't help but wonder if maybe I'm living in a dream world half the time. Who knows, maybe somebody else is bending my so-called reality to their will so they can extract valuable information from the sub-conscious reaches of my mind. Final VerdictInception is completely original both in concept and in execution of that concept. There is absolutely no point of failure in either the story, the character development, or the general pacing with this film. So, if you enjoy the kind of science-fiction, psychological thrillers that toy with the mind's understanding of the very definition of reality itself, then, this is an A-grade movie that will not fail to live up to your expectations. I give this film a rating of 10 out of 10 for best performances, best story, and best originally done visuals that I've seen in a long time.

Reviews: A masterpiece that made me realize something. Fellow writers, read on. No spoilers.
main_review: It's 2017 and I finally managed to watch Inception, twice at that. Seven years after its release, I don't think it's necessary to go over the qualities of this movie again and bore you with expletives and superlatives regarding its excellence. The rating and the rest 2000+ reviews can tell you enough about that. Instead, I decided to present you with a fresh view on Inception's essence - my own one. Stay with me and I promise you that by the end of this review, you'll see yet another layer of Inception you haven't even thought about.After seeing Inception for the second time, I realized that the primary concept of the movie - ideas, is in fact an elaborate tutorial on writing fictional characters.Inception explores ideas and the way they affect us. In our everyday lives entering one's dreams and implanting an idea would be an impossible task. However, there is one place in real life (or not so real life) where inception of ideas is inevitable - books.The author of a book isn't much different from the extractors in Inception. Because the author always works within his character's mind. He must know who his character is better than anyone else, in order to know who they will become by the end of the story.In the course of the narrative, the author leads the character along a path that foreshadows and shows them hints about the future outcome. Nothing else - just hints. The character must arrive at the designated outcome by themselves. Thus, they go through the specifically constructed challenges and obstacles, which urge them to look at the world from a different angle and maybe realize a thing or two about themselves and the people around them. The author never explicitly says "See what I did here? It's supposed to lead to this and that." because that would break the willing suspension of disbelief of both character and reader - it would draw attention to the writer. However, he covertly (and cleverly) weaves the path before his character and shows them the things that would make them question themselves and eventually lead to a change in their mindset.Yet, what drives the character forward after all? Their goal. But, let's face it - no character goal is truly that character's personal goal. Literary characters are just that - fiction. In reality, goals belong to the author who masks them so skillfully that the character believes them to be their own. After all, goals are the embodiment of a character's hopes and dreams and although their material form is usually absent at the beginning of the story, the strive to achieve them gives the character strength and perseverance. And what else in the world is intangible, yet strong enough to affect one's life? Ideas.If you are just reading books for enjoyment and not obsessively inspecting each sentence like I do, at the end of the story you will see a character that has altered their way of thinking, but you won't realize the process through which it had happened. They would have either reached their goal, or realized that it hadn't been what they actually needed. Anyway, they would be a "new person" - they would look at the world with clear eyes. When you trace it back in the story, you might be able to tell how and why (provided that you are skilled enough in literary analysis).But why is it so hard to determine the trigger of character development WHILE you are reading? Let's make it clear - it's not because you're not paying attention. A badly written story will scream "THIS IS SUPPOSED TO LEAD TO CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT!" ten pages before the actual trigger. Then what is the secret?The thing is, just major story events strung together can't lead to character development that feels natural and the story will start screaming for attention like I showed above. Moreover, characters will be one-dimensional, will seem to lack firm motivations and goals, and their emotions will feel forced.The secret lies in the small details skillfully placed at just the right moments in the narrative, which build upon one another to lead to the major events. Thereafter, the major events have greater impact and resonate into character development. Amateur writers won't notice these essential small details unless they have trained themselves to spot them through reading. They will think that the major events are the only triggers of character development. Then they will write their own stories without these key details and wonder why they won't trigger the same emotions like their favorite novels. Why they won't trigger any emotions at all. Well, now you know why.Anyway, I feel my review turned into a creative writing lecture, but Inception perfectly illustrates the way an author develops their characters. At least that's the conclusion I reached for myself and the way I saw the movie. Because I'm a writer and I filter everything through my own crazy, maniacal, writing prism. My review may not appeal to the people who came for the action sequences or the ones who simply wanted to enjoy a masterfully crafted story. However, I hope my point will reach those of you who are just as literary crazy as I am.I would prompt you to read this review after you've watched the movie, so you can see the connection between what I said and what happened in the story. Though since I'm placing this paragraph at the end of my review, it would be foolish to ask this of you, won't it? Yet again, I would prompt you to reread it after you've seen the movie. Or at least, to go into Inception with the idea in mind that it is an illustrative example of how to develop characters in fiction. The best of all examples.

It has been said that Hollywood relies too much on special effects to cover lazy storytelling; not so with Inception, where truly stunning visuals only supplement what you'll really be talking about: the story, what it means, how it moved you, and how shockingly original it is. I've never seen anything like it, either in concept or in narrative structure. Neither have I attended, in a long time, a film that gave my brain such a workout.This is a movie that expects you to pay attention and make connections. Leonardo DiCaprio gives a heartbreaking performance, leading a cast of top-notch actors playing interesting characters in a film that appears to be a science-fiction action/heist caper (a rather unique concept in itself), but is actually about guilt, the desire for redemption, and the raw power of simple ideas. Director Christopher Nolan, as he did with Batman Begins and The Dark Knight, takes something fantastic and paints it in realistic tones. This is what unbridled imagination, combined with intelligence, emotion, and talent looks like on film. It is mentally and emotionally challenging. It also has some terrific action (including a physics- bending fight sequence that is jaw-dropping) and is very creative in its use of cinematography, editing, and music. Though comparatively light on language, with no sexual material and action violence where physical harm is not what's at stake (you'll understand when you see it), Inception is nonetheless not recommended for anyone younger than teens due to its complexity and intense subject matter.

Reviews: Review of the Cinematography of Inception
main_review: Imagine you are dreaming, and you know it. You are an architect and have the power to do anything you want to your landscape. You can build skyscrapers or farm houses, you can make oceans appear out of nothing, and you can defy the laws of physics. You can go into the deepest spaces of your subconscious and see all of your fears, secrets, and desires. You can dream voluntarily and even bring other people along with you. This is Inception. Leonardo DiCaprio acts as Cobb, a thief who steals much more than everyday material items. He has the capability to steal secrets from the minds of other people through their subconscious, by invading their dreams without them knowing. While this sounds amazing, it is an enormous power to have, and with great power comes great responsibility. Cobb gets involved in a dangerous mission and is asked to plant an idea into another person's mind. He has already lost his family to his career, but if he completes this task, he could get it all back. However, he is not prepared for the emotional baggage he's kept to appear at work. Inception is a complete and total enigma. It is anything and everything that one could ever possibly imagine, but never think of themselves. It is so original in itself that there is nothing remotely close to being like it. It deserves every accolade and testimonial it is given, and while director Christopher Nolan is very responsible for that, he was not alone in creating this masterpiece. Wally Pfister is a cinematographer and director who is well known for his work with Christopher Nolan. In Inception, he uses cinematography to tell a story. It's not just about getting the perfect shot, it's about connecting the audience to the picture and the actors. With pristine clarity from every angle, viewers are immediately immersed in their surroundings. He draws them in by giving each shot a unique look from the next. Because of Inception's complicated plot line, he uses color, lighting, and shot types to his advantage in differentiating environments from one another. The component of the film that is most obvious to the viewer is lighting. In the first scene, the audience sees waves on the beach crashing into the shore. Pfister uses natural light to portray the outdoors and create a bright environment. In the next, viewers see Leonardo DiCaprio being led inside a dark building. Here, Pfister uses a dim palette with warm colors to show both the change of environment as well as the different emotions of each scene. This pattern continues as the plot unravels throughout the film.One particularly great shot Pfister uses to engage his audience is an aerial view of the environment. For the majority of the film, when the characters move into a new setting, viewers are graced with a breathtaking overhead shot of their surroundings. These wide pans show a boundless space, but usually always have a focal point. For example, while the audience sees a large, urban city that becomes the next setting of the story, they can't help but to be focused in on a small, bright helicopter flying over top of it. After seeing these wide shots viewers are drawn in once again through medium shots and close ups. Pfister also knows the importance of camera movement in the story. He constantly uses shaky camera movement when characters are walking, running, or fighting. He also uses it to make experience more real for viewers. For example, when Leonardo Dicaprio and his supporting cast are in a helicopter, the camera is gently moving, not so much to distract people from what is happening in the scene, but to enhance what is happening in the film. This strategy makes it easy for the audience to get lost in the story and connect to feel like they are in the film themselves.Another important component of the cinematography that directly relates to the story is the use of cuts. In the story, one of the ways characters realize that they are dreaming is if they cannot figure out how they have gotten to where they are. It seems as if they appear there out of thin air. Each cut pertains to this aspect of the film because they rarely offer information on how characters end up in certain places. So why is Inception such a masterpiece to even surpass the other works of the 2000's is the skill seen in every aspect of the films creation. From the sound design and musical score that is provided by the master composer Hans Zimmer to the more than praiseworthy cinematography of Wally Pfister who is at his best here in providing some of the most gorgeous shots I have ever seen in a blockbuster film like this one. I haven't even had time to mention the visuals. There are times in modern day cinema where I feel fatigued of the constant barrage of bad CGI implementation in the movies that are touted as the 'best action movie of the year' that I forget just how much of a beneficial tool it can be when used correctly. This is truly Inception's greatest asset. The many great moments of this film are a mix between the real and practical effects and the computer generated special effects that blur together in such a way that you can barely make the two apart and scenes you'll swear must have been made on a PC are made the way that film makers have been doing for nearly a century. This great uncertainty in what is real and what is not adds magic to this film that has long been becoming a rarity in this age where we truly must marvel in how a scene was done. main_review: While some people don't agree that Nolan's Inception deserves to be number 14 pm IMDb's top 250 movies of all time, I think it has many features that make it worthy of such a position. First, however, I must address the one drawback I found with the film. I think there is an objective lack of character development in the movie. Cobb, the main character, is the only character who is not a one dimensional character. The sheer number of secondary characters forces them to compete for screen time and thus hinders their own development. However, this shortcoming is, in my opinion, well outweighed by the other aspects of the film. For example, the complexity of the movie is unparalleled by most blockbuster films. While the exposition may feel contrived at points, I think Nolan challenges the audience's intellect. Many viewers need to watch the movie more than once just to fully grasp the plot. Secondly, the ambiguity of the movie opens it up to multiple interpretations, and gives film with a lasting impact on the viewer. Personally, I think a movie that has you thinking about its meaning far beyond your first viewing experience is a great movie. For example, to some viewers the movie seems to suggest that the movie itself was all a dream, but to others it may not seem so. But there is evidence for both sides. An example for the former theory is when Cobb returns to his children, and they tell him that they've been building a "house on a cliff", which is strongly associated with Saito's dreams (another secondary character), hinting at the possibility of the movie ending in a dream. However, evidence also points to the contrary, such as Cobb's wedding ring only appearing in scenes that are dreams. It's the ambiguity that allows the movie to resonate with its viewers, and it's why the film is so widely praised. Furthermore, the soundtrack deserves its share in credit. Not only does it take risks by being a pronounced part of many emotional scenes, but it was actually crafted from a single piece of music: the "French song" that signifies the end of a dream. Overall, despite its shortcomings in character development, I think this film deserves much of its critical praise, because it is complex enough to to satisfy a viewer many times over.

Reviews: a powerful film with a powerful concept.
main_review: Every once in a while a film finds its way across our screens that challenges us on several levels. Such films challenge us to think critically and pay attention. Others address issues that shake the core of human emotion. Additional films attack our senses with amazing visuals, a powerful score, or both. Christopher Nolan's Inception is a film that takes all of these elements in and turns them into a powerhouse of human emotion. The film explores the theme of the power of guilt and its subsequent ability to overtake everything that makes you yourself, while also making you question what the word reality truly means. The film stars the always powerful Leonardo DiCaprio as the films main protagonist Dom Cobb. Cobb is a man on the run from his past as well as from the country he calls home, struggling to cope with the loss of his wife and separation from his children. Cobb, along with Joseph Gordon-Levitt's character, Arthur, specialize in the extraction of memories from their victims' subconscious minds. Cobb and Arthur are so skilled at this job that they are invited by their most recent mark. The twist, it is revealed, is that he does not want a memory removed, rather he wants an idea inserted into another's mind; A job that is rewarded with nothing short of Cobb's return to his children. What ensues is Cobb's personal mission to accomplish the seemingly impossible and create perform inception on his intended mark. Inception is a film that utilizes both stunning visuals as well as Hans Zimmer's ever powerful score to navigate not only the gravity of the situations Cobb and company find themselves in, but also to explore the depth of emotion that the film resides in. Similar another seminal piece of Nolan film, Interstellar, Inception is a visual and musical delight that attacks the senses and connects the viewer(s) to the experience of the film. These films are also similar in the way that Nolan utilizes cinematography to address the theme of the film. Camera angles are a central focus in Inception, and Nolan uses them masterfully to shift focus from characters to more abstract items that help gain an attachment from his viewers on the concept of totems and their appearance. Inception is viewed by many as a masterpiece from Christopher Nolan. If begs the question of when reality stops being reality and when a dream stops being a dream. Inception also addresses the subconscious need for closure and acceptance of reality. This film stands to me as an excellent example of the power of film to excavate the deepest core feelings of the human mind and its ability to cope with its problems.

Reviews: One of the Great Modern Spectacles
main_review: Leonardo DiCaprio is the last big movie star left in the world. There may be one or two others who can still bring in big crowds, but so what. Being a movie star is about projecting an image. Bogart did that. Dean did that. Brando did that. And so does DiCaprio.Christopher Nolan is the last big auteur left in the world. No one else can get $150 million original projects off the ground, and no one else can make $150 million projects that are creative and deep and dynamic and appealing to the modern audience. He is our heir to Kubrick and Hitchcock.So it makes sense that these two team up and make a movie together. And it makes sense that said movie would be one of the greatest pieces of art of the new millennium.Inception is a movie, but it is far more than that. It is an experience that involves all parts of your mind. There isn't another film that is both this exciting, this interesting, and this intellectually pleasing. It reminds me of the first time I ever heard Beethoven's Ninth or Vivaldi's The Four Seasons.DiCaprio plays a dream thief. He and his team go into people's heads while they're asleep and steal their memories, such as codes to safes. But a powerful businessman, Saito, offers him a new challenge: inception. He must plant a thought inside the heir to a business fortune and make him believe that he came up with it naturally.As the film puts it: Arthur: "I say to you, 'Don't think about elephants.' What are you thinking about?" Saito: "Elephants." Arthur: "Right, but it's not your idea. The dreamer can always remember the genesis of the idea. True inspiration is impossible to fake." Despite what Arthur believes at first, inception is not impossible. But it is difficult. Only one man has ever done it before: DiCaprio's character, Cobb. But he never wants to do it again. At first, Saito is put back, but then he makes Cobb an offer he can't refuse. What is this offer? A chance to see his kids again and live in peace. He has been on the run ever since he was accused of killing his wife Mal.The genius of this film lies in how it dives into Cobb's psyche as he and his team dives into the heir's mind. This pays off time after time, none more so than when the atmosphere gets claustrophobic. It's like eating two decadent cakes stacked on top of each other. If this was done for its own sake, it would be effective but superfluous. But it's not; all the threads come together perfectly.The cast is incredible. Other than DiCaprio, we have Michael Caine, Tom Hardy, and two of my favorite young stars, Ellen Page and Joseph Gordon-Levitt. I wouldn't say any of them turn in the best performance of their careers, but they are all very good, especially Page, whom I actually connect with more here than I did in Juno.In any case, this is the best movie most of them will ever be in. And it just gives me a certain fanboyish sort of glee to see some of the best actors alive in one of the best movies of the decade made by one of the greatest living directors.For most people who haven't seen the movie, the first thing that comes to mind when they think of it is that blaring noise they used in every trailer from 2010-2012. It originated in the trailer for this film and spread like wildfire. That got annoying quickly. But it works in this film. It is shrill and unsettling, which fits the tone of that section of the trailer perfectly. It's no 'Time', a wonderful piece you should check out if you have even a feigning interest in orchestral music. But it is good enough.That's about how I feel about Zimmer scores in general: even at their worst, they are good enough. The closest I've ever coming to hating a Zimmer score was in Interstellar. That organ grated on me. Yes, it was narratively potent, but poor sound mixing ruined it for me. But most times, I love Zimmer scores. He's the best of the 'new', electronica-influenced composers. His scores in the Batman movies were fantastic. But he is at his best here.Many people who went to see this movie ended up seeing it two or three times. This is partially because the summer blockbuster season was notoriously vacant, and no other good movies were out. But it is also because this movie confused a lot of people, not in the 'What did I just see?' way, but in the 'That was awesome, but I didn't completely get it, so I'm going to watch it again' kind of way.This is not Nolan's most confusing and mindbending film- that would be Memento, which I actually and truly did not completely get until I played through it a few times- but it is the most confusing popular Nolan movie. Interstellar comes close, but that movie was more headscratchingly confusing than 'put the pieces of the story together' confusing.For all the rampant talk about how Nolan's movies lack a heart, this movie works because of its emotional dive into Cobb's heart. Without it, this film is simply a high-concept, amazingly inventive heist film. With it, the film is one of my favorite of all time, a movie I want to break out at every occasion possible.

The story can either be told in a few sentences, or not told at all. Here is a movie immune to spoilers: If you knew how it ended, that would tell you nothing unless you knew how it got there. And telling you how it got there would produce bafflement. The movie is all about process, about fighting our way through enveloping sheets of reality and dream, reality within dreams, dreams without reality. It's a breathtaking juggling act, and Nolan may have considered his "Memento" (2000) a warm-up; he apparently started this screenplay while filming that one. It was the story of a man with short-term memory loss, and the story was told backwards.Like the hero of that film, the viewer of "Inception" is adrift in time and experience. We can never even be quite sure what the relationship between dream time and real time is. The hero explains that you can never remember the beginning of a dream, and that dreams that seem to cover hours may only last a short time. Yes, but you don't know that when you're dreaming. And what if you're inside another man's dream? How does your dream time synch with his? What do you really know?Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) is a corporate raider of the highest order. He infiltrates the minds of other men to steal their ideas. Now he is hired by a powerful billionaire to do the opposite: To introduce an idea into a rival's mind, and do it so well he believes it is his own. This has never been done before; our minds are as alert to foreign ideas as our immune system is to pathogens. The rich man, named Saito (Ken Watanabe), makes him an offer he can't refuse, an offer that would end Cobb's forced exile from home and family.Cobb assembles a team, and here the movie relies on the well- established procedures of all heist movies. We meet the people he will need to work with: Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), his longtime associate; Eames (Tom Hardy), a master at deception; Yusuf (Dileep Rao), a master chemist. And there is a new recruit, Ariadne (Ellen Page), a brilliant young architect who is a prodigy at creating spaces. Cobb also goes to touch base with his father-in-law Miles (Michael Caine), who knows what he does and how he does it. These days Michael Caine need only appear on a screen and we assume he's wiser than any of the other characters. It's a gift.

I want to enjoy a movie in the theater or at home and then keep enjoying it because it's content or portrayal is so compelling that I find mind migrating back to scenes or experiences in the film. I do enjoy sitting down to a fun, exciting movie solely for the purpose of entertainment. Inception, however, is not one of those movies. Everyone has dreams. After watching Inception, I found myself musing on the impossibilities and possibilities of dreams. I found myself wanting write down my dreams more often. That's the kind of movie Inception is: the kind that becomes a part, even if it's a small part, of my life. It becomes a place my mind can roam to for engaging thought and feeling. Reviews: A complex yet brilliant film for the ages
main_review: For many, this film is synonymous with complexity—and rightfully so. Its intricate plot has more than just dreams within dreams but also ideas within ideas. There is more to Inception than just its plot twists, however. Inception is above all the most innovative idea to come out of Hollywood since Donnie Darko but is also an exhibition of fantastic cinematography, good acting, a moving score, and a compelling plot. There are too many unique elements to dreaming and inception in this story to cover them all, but a list of some of them would include: that five minutes in the real world gives an hour in the dream, the concept of architects who design dreams as mazes, that there are projections of the subconscious who can turn on those who do not belong in the dream, totems, that dreamers use bank vaults as places to hide secure information, the concept of a forger as someone who imitates real people within a dream rather than the conventional definition, etc. Because Inception has so many of these original ideas, all of which are new to the audience, much of the movie must be dedicated to explaining these concepts to the audience. How these ideas are explained and how much time is given to their explanation is critical to the film's success because there is a balance that must be met between providing enough information that the audience can understand what's going on but not so much that the audience is overwhelmed and loses interest in the story. Nolan's execution of this balance is flawless. By using multiple characters to teach the audience (Cobb, Arthur, and Eames) and dividing new concepts up between scenes, Nolan keeps his ideas fresh and manageable for the audience."An idea is like a virus: resilient, highly contagious. The smallest seed of an idea can grow. It can grow to define or destroy you." This is how Cobb characterizes an idea and is clearly the definition at work in the film. The audience learns about the process of inception very gradually over the course of the film. We are initially told that it is a means of planting an idea into a dreamer's head and, if successful, making them believe it is their own. Then Eames makes it clear to us that this process is very difficult to master because it requires the most basic stage of the idea in order for it to work. Lastly a much darker piece of inception is introduced: that the idea can destroy the one who receives it. Nolan intentionally leaves out this information until the final confrontation between Cobb and Mal, as it is the key to understanding what happened to Mal and the reason for Cobb's guilt. Part of the Nolan's genius in this film is the way he presents the story of the inception of Fischer and the bargain with Saito to the audience as if it were the main story of the film when really he is distracting us from the real story which is Cobb's relationship with Mal.A dream within a dream and the concept of inception are the defining characteristics of Inception for most viewers but the real heart of the film is the back story of Cobb and Mal. Throughout the film we are aware that their relationship is significant since Mal works as a multifaceted bridge between the real world, the dream world, and Cobb's memories both for Cobb and for the audience. She is the real antagonist of the film as her character is constantly at work to stop Cobb from succeeding. We see her interference in the dream world from the very beginning of the film where she tells Saito about him and attempts to torture Arthur. She is Cobb's cause of pain in the real world (the reason he cannot go home to his children) and she also haunts his memories' Ariadne discovers Cobb keeps certain memories of her locked away off an elevator in his mind ("These are memories I have to make right" he tells Ariadne.) Part of the genius of this story is that at first the audience is meant to believe that Mal and Cobb's relationship is a vehicle for explaining Cobb's character and the reason he must perform inception on Fischer to be able to go home. But towards the end of the film when Cobb enters Limbo and reveals that he performed inception on Mal which led to her suicide, we begin to realize that it's the other way around; the Inception of Fischer is just the vehicle to explain what Cobb did to Mal and the reason for his guilt. Mal is the basis for the film's theme of questioning the reality we live in and the source of doubt for Cobb and for the audience as to whether Cobb lives in the real world or whether he is still dreaming while his children keep him grounded in the real world.A film to be watched again and again, Inception is a thought-provoking, mind-bending film for the ages. Its complexity is not limited to its story, but extends to its cinematography, and its score. Inception is easily one of the most complex movies that I have ever watched in my entire life. It is apparent right off the bat how much thinking and effort must have been put in by writer and director Christopher Nolan in order to build such a structured plot. Nolan really did a phenomenal job in creating a film that really stimulates the audience to think. However, if you aren't constantly thinking and keeping up with what's going on in the film then you will lose touch with what is happening in the film in the beat of an eye. If focus is lost for even a few seconds that could leave the viewer lost and confused just because the plot is always being built upon and added to in some way throughout every second of the movie. One thing that might be harder than keeping track of the movie is explaining what it's about to others. As soon as I was finished watching the movie I tried to convince one of my friends to watch it by explaining what it's about, but I quickly realized that there's no way in doing Inception justice by trying to explain the plot and I just told her to go watch the movie. A lot of people I have talked to have told me that they had to watch the movie two or three times to be able to comprehend what the hell is going on.With that being said, if the viewer is actually able to keep track of the plot it is awesome to see how the original plot is constantly added to and modified to bring it to the level of complexity that it holds. The starting scene in the movie is actually brought from towards the ending where the main character Dom is in an unending dream world know as limbo and he is trying to find the man that will eventually lead him back to his family. The rest of the movie after that scene explains how he got there. The movie goes in depth explaining the idea of invading other people's dreams and using that skill to manipulate them. This idea of traveling through other people's dreams and looking at how the different levels of dreams work and how these dreams relate back to the victims beliefs and experiences in real life is really just a mind blowing concept and is an awesome idea to think about. It probably took Chris Nolan years to get the storyline ready and finalized just looking at how interrelated some of the aspects of the plot are to each other. The complexity of the plot wasn't the only part that made this the great movie that it is though, the execution in the acting also definitely added to the movie's splendor. Leonardo DiCaprio played his role for Dom perfectly just like he does for any movie that he's in, and it is easy to see how much thought the director put into picking actors for the specific roles that he needed because pretty much every other actor fills their role perfectly even though they aren't exactly the biggest names in the industry. I think this is a very underrated quality in actors in Hollywood because an actor should not be chosen for a role based on how much weight their name carries but more so on the basis of how well their characteristics display what you want to be displayed for the character that they are playing. I think it's obvious that Nolan and his crew realize this and took it into accounting when doing auditions.Inception definitely did a great job in bringing a new and original idea for a movie to the table and certainly reached its potential with the help of a great execution from the cast, directing, and other crew members. It was the first truly good, mind stimulating, and involving movie that I have seen in a while, and it gave me hope that maybe modern day movies aren't as bad as I thought they were and Hollywood still has the ability to entertain me.

Reviews: Delivers brains as well as bang for your buck
main_review: Inception wasn't the only time English writer-director Christopher Nolan has blown our minds with a big-budget summer blockbuster - two years before, he made The Dark Knight, which destroyed most people's pre- conceptions of what superhero movies should be made of, and showed you that movies designed to make a lot of money can work your brain as much as your heart-rate. Inception also blows the minds of it's characters, themselves barely able to keep up with the multi-level dream universe they create. It's a film that revels in it's own heavy exposition; finding visual thrills in discovering the possibilities of consciously walking through a dream, or showing you the beautiful art of dream- stealing.It follows Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio), an exiled criminal who makes his money from corporate espionage jobs bankrolled by rich CEO's. Only, Cobb applies his craft by entering people's dreams, extracting information left over by the dreamer's subconscious, usually within a locked safe or protected by projections of that subconscious. After a botched job, Cobb's target Saito (Ken Watanabe) offers him the chance to redeem himself and to go home, only the task is not to steal information, but to implant it, known as 'inception'. Saito wants Cobb to implant an idea into the head of Robert Fischer (Cillian Murphy), the heir to an energy conglomerate. Cobb alone has ever achieved inception, but it is a near impossible task, especially with the psychopathic projection of his dead wife (Marion Cotillard) stalking his subconscious.It's a dangerous and bold thing for a mainstream director to have confidence in it's audiences intelligence. If there's a main problem with Inception, it is probably that things get a little too baffling at times, as the crew delve deeper and deeper into the levels of the dream, and new rules start to apply. There is a lot of information to process here, and the film spends nearly its duration trying to explain it to us. But Nolan is a fantastic writer, and most directors would lose the audience without such expert storytelling ability and great dialogue. Thankfully, Ariadne (Ellen Page), an architecture student recommended to Cobb to design the dream world, plays as a proxy for the audience, learning as we learn.Ariadne is one of a bunch of experts lined up for the job - Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is Cobb's right-hand man and the brains behind the job, Eames (Tom Hardy) is a skilled in-dream impersonator, and Yusuf (Dileep Rao) is a chemist who provides a knockout drug so powerful that the dreamers cannot be shaken awake. There's also Tom Berenger, Michael Caine, Lukas Haas and Pete Postlethwaite in the mix, making this a huge ensemble. As expected, Nolan keeps tabs on them all, never allowing you to forget about anyone or about what the role they have to play. It's a miracle he even managed to line up such an impressive group of actors, let alone make sure no-one gets lost amongst the thick plot.Although the climax gets a little too over-crowded in the final half an hour, and Nolan places us in the pretty dull setting of a snowy mountain, this is still innovative, stylish and exciting action cinema. It still abides by all the standard rules of the genre, but it dares to toy with them and to keep the action moving with intriguing sub-plots or simply delivering an exceptional set-piece (Arthur's no-gravity hallway fight comes to mind). It bends the mind as much as it bends the rules, and this is much about the strangeness of dreams and what it means to dream them. Nolan went on to deliver an ever better movie two years later with The Dark Knight Rises (2012), and I'm eagerly awaiting his upcoming Interstellar (2014). He alone has reawakened my faith in the 'big' movie, proving that films can deliver brains as well as bang for your buck.www.the-wrath-of-blog.blogspot.com

Inception is a 2010 science fiction film written, co-produced, and directed by Christopher Nolan. The film stars a large ensemble cast that includes Leonardo DiCaprio, Ken Watanabe, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Marion Cotillard, Ellen Page, Tom Hardy, Dileep Rao, Cillian Murphy, Tom Berenger, and Michael Caine. DiCaprio plays Dom Cobb, a thief who commits corporate espionage by infiltrating the subconscious of his targets. He is offered a chance to regain his old life as payment for a task considered to be impossible: "inception", the implantation of another person's idea into a target's subconscious. Inception has received wide critical acclaim and numerous critics have praised its originality, cast, score, and visual effects. It won Academy Awards for Best Cinematography, Best Sound Editing, Best Sound Mixing, and Best Visual Effects, and was nominated for four more: Best Picture, Best Original Score, Best Art Direction, and Best Original Screenplay.

Inception is truly one of a kind. A concept which has long gestated in Christopher Nolan's mind, his eye for drama mixed with his large scale sensibilities ring true in Blockbuster season making Inception a true original in the sea of reboots, remakes and sequels.To try and explain Inceptions many plot twists and incredibly intelligent arcs, would be a foolish task. As Nolan himself has been reluctant to. The best way to approach the film would be with an open mind, if you are prepared to be taken on a ride of a lifetime, then trust that you 100% will. If Avatar was a seminal film in technology (although coming out as a rather poor film, in my opinion), then Inception is seminal in it's storytelling. With a 148 minute running time, you would expect a lot to take place, but what you wouldn't expect is the pace of it all. I did not think at one time in the film about how long was left. I was simply blown away by the depth in every single part of the film. If my enthusiasm for the storytelling aspect of the film has left you worried about the spectacle, then don't worry. They are, as hinted in the trailer, incredible, looking real and unbelievable simultaneously. The most pleasing thing about the action set pieces, is that they are genuinely used to illustrate the story, rather than to blow stuff up a la Michael Bay.With this complex movie in it's high concept, a stellar cast is needed. And Nolan as always, delivers with just that. The rest of the cast members all shine in parts of the films, Cillian Murphy shows off his usually non-existent tender side, Gordon-Levitt bottles his usual charm for his confidently reserved turn as the reliable Arthur, Watanabe is devilish as the seemingly ambiguous Saito, Page shows why she's the next big female star and Tom Hardy revels in being the comic relief of the film compared to his recent turns as decidedly psychopathic characters.Overall, Nolan has indeed surpassed himself. He has created a world as expansive as his Gotham, a plot dwarfing the intricacies of Memento and one which blows The Prestige's cinematic reveal out of the water. This is truly unmissable cinema. Revel in it, we've still got to wait a whole two years before Batman 3.

Reviews: The film held my interest, kept me in suspense, and made me question whether or not it would be possible for extraction or inception to occur.
main_review: The 2010 science fiction film "Inception" was written, co-produced, and directed by Christopher Nolan. "Inception" has large ensemble cast, including Leonardo DiCaprio as Dominick "Dom" Cobb, the extractor. He is a professional thief specializing in stealing secrets by infiltrating the dreams of his victims. Ken Watanabe stars as Mr. Satio. He is a Japanese businessman who hires Cobb and his team for a very specific job. Joseph Gordon-Levitt stars as Arthur one of the members of Cobb's team. Ellen Page, who I loved in "Juno", stars as Ariadne the newest member of Cobb's team. Marion Cotillard plays Mal. Mal is Dom Cobb's deceased wife. Cillian Murphy stars as Robert Michael Fischer, Jr. He is the only heir to a business empire, and Cobb's next target, the victim that Mr. Satio has hired Cobb to infiltrate. The cast includes several additional members including Michael Caine, from "The Cider House Rules", as Professor Stephen Miles, Cobb's father-in-law. The story centers on Mr. Satio's desire to have Cobb and his team infiltrate the mind of Robert Michael Fischer, Jr. through a level of dreams to plant an idea in his subconscious, the act of inception. Cobb must except this job, and complete the task at hand, if he hopes to be reunited with his children. The story takes many twists and turns throughout the film.The theme of the story is the idea that people can share a dream. Not only can a dream be shared, but information can be extracted from one individual's mind by another individual, through a dream. This idea is taken a step further by suggesting that in addition to extracting information; it is also possible for one individual to plant an idea into the subconscious mind of another individual. This film explores the reality of such a process, as well as, the dangers involved in performing the act. The film addresses the serious ramifications of such a manipulation. If I were to relate "Inception" to another film of the same genre, I would choose "The Matrix". In "The Matrix" the mind is also manipulated. The method may not be the same, but dangers to the mind certainly exist in both films.Many scenes were shot in slow motion to allow the viewer to follow the action. This technique was used to stretch the moment and intensify the effectiveness of the scene. In some scenes, the use of slow motion exaggerated the actors' movements. The viewer is then able to see the exhaustion or frustration of the characters, while they try to accomplish certain tasks. Sound was often used to intensify the transition from one scene to another. At various times throughout the film, sound was used to build suspense or set the tone. The film began with intense music. I could feel the suspense building.Although I am not a big fan of science fiction films, I felt that "Inception" was well made. I thought that Leonardo DiCaprio was outstanding in this film. He was believable as Dom Cobb. The film held my interest, kept me in suspense, and made me question whether or not it would be possible for extraction or inception to occur.

Reviews: to dream or not to dream
main_review: Inception is a film produced in 2010. The film is about Dominic Cobb and his road to recovery of almost everything he lost. Inception is set in the distant future, where they have developed a machine to enter someone's subconscious or their dreams. Dominic is one of the first persons to use this technique. After the suicide of his wife, Cobb found out a few things about dreams. Namely, people could lose their mind while invading dreams because they are unsure whether they are dreaming or awake, and secrets can be extracted from dreams. Cobb uses the knowledge he has on dreams to create a criminal organisation that enters the dreams of people to steal secrets and because of this and the strange suicide of his wife, he becomes a wanted criminal. While doing one of their schemes, it backfires and they are found out. Mr Saito, the man who captures Cob and Arthur (one of Cobb's friends that help him with stealing the ideas from the dreams), has a proposition for him. He asks him to plant an idea in someone's head instead of stealing it. Cobb wants to turn it down but he is offered a reward he can't turn down: his criminal status would be removed so he would be able to go home again and see his kids. Obviously this summary hasn't spoiled the end yet and hopefully it made you curious to find out the rest of the story. Inception is a science fiction thriller with quite some action. Even if you do not like thrillers, Inception still has a great plot, some amazing stunts and special effects that you wouldn't want to miss. The first great thing about this film would be the plot line. The plot is amazing; you are really drawn into the story of Cob and his impossible quest. The plot is not one straight line; it twists and turns like a river, especially when you watch the film for the second time. The first time you watch Inception, it is just a great film with some very cool action thrown in. The second time you watch it you will notice interesting details that you had missed out the first time and will make you rethink everything that happened. Those details make the film very realistic and you will start thinking about the whole concept of dreams. What do you dream about? Are there really secrets hidden in our subconscious? And how could you control your dreams? Another thing that makes this film amazing would be the special effects. Those special effects are very important because most of the time in the film was spent inside different dreams in different people. Everybody dreams, so you will know that in your dreams anything could happen. You dream of impossible things, and everybody has different dreams. That is exactly why special effects are so important in Inception. It explains why the film could only be produced this recent. Ten years ago, we did not have the knowledge and techniques yet to do justice to the dream world. Nowadays, a lot more can be made with CGI (computer generated imagery) and Nolan used it for quite a bit of shots, but not for everything. Where other directors would use a green screen, Nolan would try to do most of the things with stunts and a real décor. For example, there was this fighting scene in a hallway that was rotating. Nolan created a real rotating hallway and made the actor play the scene while the hallway really was turning. The actor commented that he was very glad that Nolan made him do this: not only was it a lot of fun to do it, but it was a lot more realistic than just hanging him on a contraption and tell him to act like he was off-balance. Others would just put the actors in front of a green screen and let them play their parts, but not Nolan. He is convinced that doing real stunts without a dream screen is a lot better than a green screen, and does the most extreme things to realize these. There is just one small drawback on Inception, which is that it is a very long film. The film is more than two hours long. That is quite some time to stay concentrated on one thing, especially if it is as complicated as this film. If you have a small attention span while watching it and you miss some information, it is quite a challenge to get what is going on during the rest of the movie. That said, it really is the only drawback. Of course there is always the pause button, or you could of just rewind parts of the film. But then again, because it's so difficult, you concentrate intensely on the film and most don't even notice that it's so long. All in all Inception was a great film even though it was very long. The special effect and stunt were very convincing especially the ones that took place inside the dreams. The combination of the two was superb. Add the plot and you have the best thriller of the year. Or, Inception combined so many plot elements that one could consider it to be a drama, or an action, and it even contained comical elements. Leonardo diCaprio, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Ellen Page, Ken Watanabe, Marion Cotillard and Michael Caine form a very impressive cast. Inception is a film that nearly everyone would like, except for people who watch films to relax. Cobb's story will hunt you for a long time, both in your dreams and normal life.

Yet it all revolves around it's main character, played wonderfully by Leonardo DiCaprio, who struggles with his own demons as he tries to orchestrate this dream caper. Reviews: Ideas are the most dangerous virus that exists.
main_review: Dom Cobb is an extractor who steals people's secrets while they are sleep. He is best in his field and is held in high regard, but this is also made him internationally wanted criminal. After one job went bad, he gets the chance for redemption when he has to plant an idea into someone's mind. Cobb assembles a team of specialists for his last mission. Same time he has to fight with secrets from his past that might endanger the assignment and those who work with him.I have too often heard comparisons between 'Inception' and 'The Matrix' than it is justified. Besides spectacular visual style that combines CGI with practical special effects, and that the action takes place on several levels, there aren't many other parallels. With this, I'm not trying to say that one film is superior to the other. 'Inception' stands quite in its league as an ambitious, but not a pretentious movie with an interesting concept. Thought out screenplay and world-building doesn't get confusing even when we are shown events happening three or four levels simultaneously. Yet, things are not overly simplistic, but the viewers have to concentrate fully on what is happening on the screen not to lose track. The plot is intelligent, but not convoluted, events movie on with head-spinning speed, yet there is plenty of breathing room for characters to develop. All plot points are not overly explained by the characters, but rather unveil naturally in the course of actions allowing the audience to make their assumptions. Some complain that the dreams were too logical and realistic compared to the real world, but in this case, I think, adding the layer of surrealism to the dreams would have turned the film too confusing and taken away the credibility of the film's logic that was so carefully constructed. These are not quite real dreams, but rather dreams built by architects where extractors take their targets. With this, we learn that constructing a dream can be as difficult as, we already know, writing a good screenplay. Fast-moving story together with the exciting visual style makes the two and a half hours pass without noticing because you are captivated by everything that happens on the screen.Though the last time I watched 'Inception' was almost ten years ago when it was first released, and back then I wasn't much in the awe as I perhaps wanted to be. I guess, over the time when all the hype has faded, I was able to see the film just as it is and, thus enjoy it more. Although I liked the film more and despite the intelligent writing and well-structured screenplay, stylish visuals, top-notch acting, and direction, 'Inception' still couldn't make my mind and soul chime in pure excitement. Still, I think Christopher Nolan is one of the few true visionaries in film today, and there is no doubt that 'Inception' has stood the test of time (it might be gotten even better). In the future, I am sure, it will be continued to be looked at as one of the most masterful action thrillers of time and not only that.

A story so esoteric and complex will always leave itself open for those looking for plot holes and inconsistencies. I've read many a negative review describing these things that are, admittedly, not without merit. The naysayers have lots of good points, but I'll also argue that, considering them as I watch I this movie for the umpteenth time, for every point that removes a brick, I can easily come up with a counterpoint that replaces it (and this is one of those truly rare films that shows you something new with each viewing, making you discard one thing for another and then switch it back again).In my humble opinion, Inception earns the hard won award for the most original and thought-provoking film I may ever see, topping even The Matrix in its ambition. I have yet to revisit this masterpiece and not consider at least one aspect or idea I may or may not have missed the previous time. Much like my own most enjoyable recurring dreams, it seems to mutate subtly to feel ephemeral and, at the same time, everlasting in its impact. I struggle to think of how anybody could have thought of something that seems as fantastical, bombastic and so rooted in what I can consider possible. It's like a philosophical epiphany. Or the most magnificent drug-induced trip.I'll admit, it is difficult to fully relate to the characters as the dialogue almost exclusively revolves around explaining the intricacies of the physics and logistics of being a dreamworld mercenary and, as long as it's runtime ends up being, it hurries from one development to the next, forcing you to keep up or fall behind. Such is the drawback of making something of this magnitude. Then again, you never remember the minute details of a dream, only how you felt and what you were trying to seek out. And that is exactly what Di Caprio's character is trying to accomplish. The special effects do a wonderful job of distracting from this nagging feeling, as well as another pitch perfect score from Hans Zimmer.Movies are essentially an escape, at least for me because that's what I crave. This is the closest to a waking dream I've ever been.

Nolan helms and pens a sublime science fiction thriller. This film has outstanding direction, cinematography, screenplay, settings, score and acting. The score plays just as an important role as the characters as it creates a thrilling and intense tone to the film. All of the artists involved deliver superlative performances. In particular Page, Gordon-Levity, Murphy, Hardy, Watanabe, Cotillard and Caine are superb. However it is DiCaprio who commands the screen. The plot is so complex, but I'll try to sum it up concisely keeping in mind I'll be leaving out intricate details. A powerful Japanese business man Saito wants an idea planted in the mind of the heir, Robert, to his competitor's energy conglomerate so that Robert will dissolve the company when he takes over control. Saito bribes Cobb who is an extractor to do the job. Typically an extractor is part of a team that performs corporate espionage by infiltrating the subconscious through a shared dream world and then stealing valuable information. Basically they are thieves for hire. Cobb has a criminal past which prevents him from entering the U.S. to see his children which Saito can fix with his powerful influence, so Cobb accepts the job. Cobb and his partner Arthur enlist the help of a conman Eames, a chemist Yusef who creates a sedative to create a stable dreamworld and Ariande who is an architect that builds the puzzle of the dream's landscape. In order to wake up from a dream a member from the team must stay behind at each level to set up a kick which awakens the remaining sleeping members. If a dreamer does not wake up from the kick they are stuck in Limbo which is nearly impossible to escape from and the dreamer doesn't even realize they are still in a dream. A dreamer has an object called a totem which distinguishes the dream world from reality. Cobb and his team are going to try to do what has never been done before successfully. Plant an idea in Robert's mind during a 10 hour flight which requires planting an idea by invading a dream within a dream within a dream. This will also require a simultaneous kick to awaken the team members from the multi-level dream at the same time. Cobb reveals that he and his wife Mal had been stuck in Limbo when first experimenting with dream technology and built a world which she refused to leave and come back to reality. She is stuck in Cobb's mind as a projection. The team is pulling off the mission with Mal attempting to subterfuge it at every angle. Saito ends up getting injured and death in a dream results in Limbo. The team members all awake from the simultaneous kick except for Cobb who stays behind to find an aged Saito. He uses his totem to remind Saito of their agreement. The plot is intense, thrilling, mind-blowing, intelligent, duplicitous, ingenious, cathartic and has an ambiguous ending. I had to watch this mind- bending labyrinth film a few times to truly understand and appreciate it's brilliance. In this viewer's opinion it is Nolan's masterpiece and is at the very top if not the best film in it's genre.

Inception is written, produced, and directed by Christopher Nolan. The film stars Leonardo DiCaprio, Ken Watanabe, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Marion Cotillard, Ellen Page, Tom Hardy, Cillian Murphy, Dileep Rao, Tom Berenger, and Michael Caine. The musical score is by Hans Zimmer and Wally Pfister is the cinematographer. Plot finds DiCaprio playing Dom Cobb, a specialised spy for hire who steals ideas from the dreams of people. But one day he gets a different offer, one that will enable him to see his estranged children. To get his reward he must enact Inception, the planting of an idea in the mind of the selected target. But Inception is thought impossible and should Cobb and his selected team fail? The consequences are unthinkable.There has already been much written and pondered about as regards Inception in the relatively short running time of its life. One can only imagine what will be written and said about it in ten years time. For although it's arguably a bit too early to be talking about it being held in such high regards as the likes of 2001: A Space Odyssey, it's inescapable that Nolan's movie is this current generation's sci-fi classic. That Nolan has managed to make it accessible to the mainstream, and dazzled the eyes as much as the brain in the process, is close to being a piece of genius craftsmanship.Inception is a film that it's better to know nothing about before venturing into it, and then it asks, well Nolan asks, for your undivided attention. It's neither as confusing as some have painted it, nor does it have any tricks-peek behind the curtain type-up its sleeve. The truth is is that Inception has something for everyone; thematically speaking, and that's before we pore over the special effects that sees Nolan raising the bar considerably. As is the case with twisty high concept movies, interpretations are many, with the director rightly abstaining from discourse about his movie. What forms the basis is your basic life and death struggles, with the grey areas during and after given a clever cinematic make over. There's also meditations on grief that this reviewer personally found easy to get involved with; that of course wont work for everyone, but that is just one of many strands that Nolan dangles for the discerning viewer.If that all sounds a bit too serious for the man who has redefined the Super Hero genre, rest assured thrill seekers, Inception is also a loud swirly spectacle. The action is raucous, be it gun fights or zero gravity punch ups, Nolan has not lost the ability to take the viewer on an action fuelled roller-coaster ride, aided superbly by Lee Smith's editing and Pfister's perfectly broad photography While Zimmer's score blends electronic action pulse beats with saddened guitar strains (ex-Smiths guitarist Johnny Marr on 12 string) to craft one of the best scores of 2010. As I said, there's something for everyone here, making it perhaps one of the leading nominees for title of ultimate modern day blockbuster.Then there's the strong ensemble cast, led by a quite scintillating performance from DiCaprio. Following on from his cards played close to his chest turn in Shutter Island, DiCaprio has given 2010 two of its best lead performances. Here he gives real depth of emotion, the kind that makes it easy for the viewers to hang their hats on. His unfussy acting is easy to buy into, giving the character the air of believability, he is the glue that binds the whole film together. Murphy is wonderfully vulnerable, very much an axis in the narrative, while Levitt almost usurps DiCaprio with a neatly layered portrayal that carries a delightful whiff of duality about it. Special praise, too, for Ellen Page. Still in her early 20s, she exudes an intelligent sexiness that shines bright in a role that could have been boorishly played as a cipher in a lesser actress' hands. While Hardy provides brawny levity and Berenger leaves a favourable mark.The Matrix meets Heat and Mission Impossible, only it's written by Phillip K. Dick and Richard Matheson; or something like that. A cracking hybrid movie that's fit to grace any summer and sure to improve and enlighten with further viewings.

Nolan, Nolan, Nolan. Where do I start?How can I start?I have to say that I usually do not refer to other movies while comparing and I'll rate this movie as an experience alone. Inception by far is the best cinema I have seen to date and I'll tell you why. The sheer brilliance of it is mind blowing. The idea of corporate espionage via dream sharing is by far the craziest and yet the most spectacular idea of this decade. When I heard about this movie I was like, "Oh cool, another Sci-Fi movie." Then the trailer came out and we saw a whole city bending on its own and I was like, "Gotta watch that movie.". Inception excels in storyline and visuals better than practically every other movie. The sheer idea of nested dream sharing is beyond the thinkable and the execution of the movie is remarkable. By far Nolan's best work, and even as a Nolan fan from the era of The Dark Knight, I have to say, this movie exceeds even his own The Dark Knight in many ways. First off, this movie explores the mind itself in ways that allows us to visualize what our subconscious thinks. The movie gives us a better understanding of ourselves as humans and truly is a remarkable feat of cinematography. The sheer ambition of the movie itself is enough to get you on the edge of your seat. Leave the visuals, the scoring is daunting. Hans Zimmer at work again uses the tick tock metronome again to perfection and the blaring horns that make us fall off our seats. And who even expected that JACK from the Titanic would end up performing the role of an Corporate Thief perfectly? The acting is beyond sublime and truly the movie Inception is by far my favorite movie till date.However, Inception does lack minorly. There are a few plotholes in the movie, but in the expanse of less than three hours, their is very little Inception doesn't achieve. If anything the only place where Inception lacks is in character development and storyline. I have so little against this movie and I have to say, this movie is a feat in cinematic history. Overall, this movie is a must watch for anyone. An incredible thriller and emotional story. Inception truly delivers an awesome cinematic experience.

Reviews: Awesome Effects, Try and Keep Up!
main_review:
Cristopher Nolan's Inception is quite grasping in the sense that you can't look away for long or you may lose your grip on the storyline. There are plenty of action packed scenes with out of this world digital effects to keep your attention, but the reason we lock our eyes to this film is truly to keep up with it. Taking us in and out of many of the characters including Dom Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio), Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), Mal (Marion Cotillard), Mr. Saito (Ken Watanabe), and Robert Fischer's (Cillian Murphy) dream state and subconscious, we are forced to engage the analytical portions of our brain in an effort to stay with the story. 
The overall theme of the movie came in mixed signals, leaving me initially unable to decide whether the film was centered around corporate espionage, a father's willingness to do anything to see his children, or learning to let go of the past. After some more thought, I have to go with a father's willingness to do anything to see his children again. Mostly due to the fact that the majority of the film in which they are trying to plant an idea in Robert Fischer's head was spawned as a result of the decision Dom made to accept the job in an effort to see his children again. Thereafter and even before, there are scenes that cut to projections of his children as he can't seem to shake them or his dead wife's subconscious projection. The dream glow lighting effects used in these projections of his children are enough to make you feel his pain and sadness further emphasizing the reason he has taken an almost impossible job to get back to them. These repetitious projections provide a motif that is evenly spread throughout the film in an effort to remind us why he is there in the first place.
As you are taken either gracefully or forcefully from one scene to the next in the many altered dream state realities, Cristopher Nolan does a fantastic job making sure part of you goes with the character while you also remain thoughtful of the true reality of the dreamer and those along for the ride. The digital effects in most scenes are astounding and the thoughtful use of various speeds of slow motion to produce the effect and understanding of their dream state was masterfully done. This is especially apparent during the crux of the film as they immerse themselves into a three-level deep dream state in which each level's time passes differently in hours, days, months, or years! Overall, this film is a pretty mind-blowing work of art that goes way beyond our imagination to show just how far a father will go for his children.

Reviews: Dreams or reality? This movie almost depicts them the same!
main_review:
Christopher Nolan seems to have forgotten the most important aspect of a dream: dreams are chaotic and have no logic.
The depiction of dreams is just wrong. I would have understood if he used another concept... I don't know... alternative realities or implanting the logic of reality into a dream (for example physics and character behavior and control from the real world), lucid dreaming or even the sleep paralysis state (where you are fully aware of your dreams that are projected into the real world, and you can control them). No, here is just the concept of dreams. All the dreams are action-based (really now?), they look normal, everyone seems to control them perfectly; everything is very well organized. Also, the physics match the real world; the presence of paradoxical architecture and other minor key elements are a positive thing here (but not enough to make a well-depicted dream).
Too bad. This movie had great potential and contained an interesting plot.
I also feel that the possible twist at the end was unnecessary. This is probably Christopher Nolan's weakest movie.
Only David Lynch can handle the concepts and philosophy of dreams.
